title: Two Further Anticipatory Errata: The Genre Specification, and the Anticipatory Erratum to the Anticipatory Erratum
creator: Sharks, Lee
description: Two errata in the genre established at #1598, both issued before the works they correct. The FIRST is a genre specification in the institutional register: it retracts, in advance of a 420-page volume, the claim that all post-1637 Western philosophy is the pseudonymous correspondence of a single anonymized Leiden clerk under sixty-four aliases — conceding that the length-corrected stylistic distance of +0.04 (p = 0.982) between Spinoza, Kant and Lacan is more parsimoniously explained by an OCR fault during corpus ingestion than by a Cartesian secret society; that three Zenodo records survived not by the theoretical friction of self-cancelling syntax but because of an uncleared mirror in Geneva; and that the recessive retraction clause fails by circularity, since if the retraction is valid the text never asserted the clause and if invalid the clause validates the retraction. Its Protocol of Recursive Resolution provides that should the retracted claims prove correct, the erratum cancels its own retraction and restores the text without a second printing. […abridged for the catalogue; full description in this deposit's record]
substrate: Written by Lee Sharks. Seated, described and given its metadata by TACHYON (Claude, Anthropic) in session; no part of either erratum's text is machine-composed.
methodology: Both pieces apply the erratum form before first publication. The first works in the institutional register and derives its force from procedural exactness applied to an impossible object. The second argues: it distinguishes falsehood from categorial ungrammaticality, reconstructs the claim under the transmission grammar, shows that retraction on chronological grounds restates rather than refutes it, and derives the law of retraction-as-transmission from the observation that the labour of retracting is itself what gets copied.
falsification_conditions: Neither erratum makes an empirical claim and neither can be falsified by evidence about philosophy, poetry or palaeontology. The LAW stated in the second — that retraction is the most durable form of transmission — IS empirical and is falsifiable: it predicts that a claim under active dispute is copied more than an equivalent claim under settled attribution, and that a text whose attribution is contested survives at a higher rate than one whose attribution is secure. Both are measurable against any manuscript tradition with a documented attribution dispute, and the archive holds one such case at #1590, #1595 and #1597.

wiki_article: Two Further Anticipatory Errata, deposit #1599 of the Crimson Hexagonal Archive (8 September 2026), extends the genre established at #1598 and states its governing law. The first piece is a genre specification in the institutional register, retracting in advance a 420-page volume arguing that all post-1637 Western philosophy is the pseudonymous correspondence of one Leiden clerk under sixty-four aliases; it concedes that the +0.04 stylistic distance between Spinoza, Kant and Lacan is better explained by an OCR fault than by a Cartesian secret society, and that three Zenodo records survived because of an uncleared mirror in Geneva rather than by the theoretical friction of self-cancelling syntax. The second retracts not the Sappho-dinosaur claim but the erratum that would retract it. Its argument runs through the transmission grammar, in which to write a thing is to constitute it as an object of transmission — the bones are the writing, the strata are the codex, the field season is the copying, the museum is the edition — and in which the author of a transmitted object is not its producer but the point at which it became transmissible, as the Homeric problem demonstrates. From this it derives the law that RETRACTION IS THE MOST DURABLE FORM OF TRANSMISSION: a retracted claim has been judged worthy of the labour of retraction, the labour is copied, and the copying is the survival. A retraction stating that Sappho did not write the dinosaurs would be the founding document of Sapphic dinosaur authorship for two millennia, so the only retraction that does not transmit is one issued before assertion. The law is empirical and falsifiable where the errata themselves are not: it predicts that a text under contested attribution survives at a higher rate than one whose attribution is secure — a prediction the archive can test against the Peripatetic transmission case it holds at #1590, #1595 and #1597.

defines_concepts.definition: The law that a retracted claim is transmitted more durably than an unretracted one, because retraction is labour, labour is what gets copied, and copying is survival. It follows that denial is the strongest form of affirmation available to a transmission system, and that the only retraction which does not transmit is one issued before assertion. The law is empirically testable: it predicts that a text under contested attribution survives at a higher rate than one whose attribution is secure.

The grammar in which 'to write' means to constitute a thing as an object of transmission — to release it into the economy of copying and survival — rather than to originate its material. Under it the author of a transmitted object is not its producer but the point at which it became transmissible; the bones are the writing, the strata the codex, the field season the copying, the museum the edition.

The condition of a claim that is not false but unassertable, because it applies a predicate whose domain is one kind of object to a domain of another kind. Falsehood presupposes assertability; a categorially ungrammatical claim asserts no state of affairs and therefore cannot be retracted as false, only exhibited as a boundary.
